newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Romania pushes case for NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: Romania pushes case for NATO membership.

text.p: Romanian President Emil Constantinescu, on the second day of a trip to Brussels, pushed the case on Tuesday for his country to be admitted to NATO in the first round of its planned eastwards expansion.
"The only course for Romania is integration," Constantinescu told a meeting of NATO's 16 ambassadors.

Constantinescu, who has committed his country to a bold economic reform plan since triumphing over ex-communists in elections last November, said his country was now back on the path to a western-style democracy.
"1996 was the year in which Romania achieved its political maturity," he said, adding his people had demonstrated by his election their firm desire for membership of the European Union and NATO.

The president was given a sympathetic hearing by the NATO allies, impressed by his centrist coalition's commitment to reform and the diligence with which it has tried to bring its military into line with NATO requirements.

"The manner in which the (November presidential) election took place is evidence of the attachment of your country to democratic and pluralist values," NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said in a welcoming address, adding:
"In a little time, Romania has truly come a very long way."

Romania, though still a dark horse, has recently joined Slovenia as two outsiders thought to have a real chance of being asked to join the alliance along with favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic at a special summit in Madrid in July.
A succession of western politicians have recently visited Bucharest to express support for the new government.

On Monday, the European Commission said the EU could unblock 70 million Ecus ($83 million) in balance of payments aid for Romania once the country had reached an agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in loan talks.
Constantinescu wants World Bank, IMF and EU support for a radical free-market reform package which includes a privatisation drive.
Both the IMF and World Bank withheld or suspended credits over the previous government's dismal reform record.

Inflation soared to 57 percent last year -- more than triple the target agreed with the IMF -- and the state budget gap is believed to have bulged to 5.7 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP) against a 2.2 percent forecast.
